one_liner: Julia's default sort! on Int32 radix-sorts a 400k-element array 8.5x faster than C++ std::sort in LangArena Sort::Self.
what_it_does: LangArena's Sort::Self test copies a 400,000-element array of pseudo-random integers in 0..999,992 and sorts it with each language's built-in sort, 50 times. The Julia program is a plain sort!(copy(data)) on a Vector{Int32}, and C++ calls std::sort on a std::vector<int32_t>. The catalogued 'implementation' is Julia's standard-library sort dispatch (base/sort.jl), not a separate library: in Julia it is a drop-in default, and from C++ there is nothing to call.
how_it_is_fast: Julia's default sort for vectors runs a decision tree (_DEFAULT_ALGORITHMS_FOR_VECTORS: InitialOptimizations, IsUIntMappable, Small{40}, CheckSorted, ComputeExtrema, ConsiderCountingSort, ConsiderRadixSort). Here the range 999,992 is not below div(399,999, 2), so counting sort is skipped. 20 bits + 70 < 22 ln(399,999), which is about 284, so it commits to an LSD radix sort over the 20-bit offset from the minimum (base/sort.jl v1.13.1). That is linear-time radix sorting against libstdc++'s comparison-based introsort. The win is algorithm choice in the standard library, not JIT code quality; the suite's own docs/ai_critic.js says 'You're comparing algorithms, not languages.'
when_to_use: In Julia, sorting large Vector{Int32}, Vector{Int64}, Float or other UInt-mappable element types with the default ordering: plain sort! already picks counting or radix sort, so no package is needed.

As a reminder to C++ developers that the speedup is available in C++ too: for integer keys, swap std::sort for a radix or SIMD sort such as Boost.Sort spreadsort, ska_sort, Highway vqsort or x86-simd-sort (all catalogued).
When arrays are in the hundreds of thousands of elements and the key range is narrow relative to n, where Julia's heuristic chooses counting or radix sort.
when_not_to_use: As evidence that a JIT beats AOT C++: in the same suite's same-algorithm tests Julia loses (Sort::Quick Julia/Default 1.307 s vs C/Gcc 1.15 s; Sort::Merge 1.602 s vs C/Clang 1.09 s).
With a custom lt/by ordering or a non-UInt-mappable element type: the IsUIntMappable branch falls back to ScratchQuickSort, so the radix path and this speedup do not apply.
For small arrays (insertion sort below 40 elements) or wide key ranges with few elements, where bits + 70 >= 22 ln(n) sends Julia to a comparison sort.
Under memory pressure: radix sort allocates an n-element scratch buffer per call, and the Julia process peaks at about 405 MB against 8.6 MB for C++ in this test.
When you need the fastest comparison sort: even Rust's built-in t.sort() takes 0.410 s here, 2.4x faster than std::sort, so std::sort is a weak reference point (derived from page data).

integration.dependencies: none (Julia Base.Sort); the LangArena harness itself uses JSON3 and Printf
integration.min_toolchain: Julia with the ComputeExtrema/ConsiderRadixSort default pipeline (present in base/sort.jl v1.13.1; a code comment there dates the radix path to the v1.9 development cycle); measured on Julia 1.13.1
integration.platforms: any Julia platform; measured on x86-64 (AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, Linux)
integration.thread_safety: sort! mutates its argument in place, single-threaded; concurrent sorts of distinct vectors are independent (no shared state documented)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — sort! is Julia's default, so Julia code gets it automatically; it is not callable as a std::sort replacement from C++

gotchas: Harness quirk: the 'random' input comes from the Benchmarks Game LCG (IM = 139968, IA = 3877, IC = 29573 in cpp/src/helper.hpp), whose full period is 139,968. The 400,000-element array is therefore the same 139,968-value sequence repeated about 2.86 times, with every value occurring 2 or 3 times (checked by re-running the generator). This affects both sides equally and does not invalidate the comparison, but the input is not 400k independent random keys.
Not the same algorithm: the 8.5x is radix sort against introsort. The verifier capped the entry at C for this reason, and a C++ radix sort would be the fair comparison.

One measurement per test and configuration, no variance; the headline C++ row is the -O2 'prod' build, but -O3 -march=native ('Fast', 0.998 s) and PGO (0.999 s) do not help std::sort. The Julia harness forces GC.gc() before the timed loop, and both sides run untimed warm-up iterations (20% of the timed count) before timing.

The results file notes say the host switched from Ubuntu to Arch Linux, yet the reported gcc is an Ubuntu-packaged trunk snapshot (16.0.1 20260322, experimental), so the exact toolchain provenance is unclear.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this only to show that a managed language's standard library can choose a better algorithm by default. Among the LangArena siblings, the OpenJDK Binarytrees::Obj and Calculator::Ast rows compare like-for-like algorithms and say more about the runtime itself. The Julia (no BLAS) matmul entry is a similar algorithm and loop-structure mismatch.
verified_claims_summary: On an AMD Ryzen 7 3800X (LangArena results 2026-10-05, one run per configuration), 50 sorts of a copied 400,000-element Int32 array take 0.116 s with Julia 1.13.1's default sort! against 0.982 s with g++ 16.0.1 -O2 std::sort, the best of the 16 C/C++ configurations: about 8.5x (derived from page data). C's qsort-with-callback rows take 1.96-2.03 s (instrumented PGO builds excluded).
status_note: LangArena is active (monthly result files, MIT, 41 stars) and calls itself a subjective benchmark. The Julia behaviour is the standard-library default and needs no integration, but the comparison is an algorithm win capped at tier C.
